iw: Bans the largest campuses, though none were proposed there

w: Senate President Stuart Adams and developer Kevin O'Leary
t: Adams demands 75% Stratos cut; O'Leary agrees to halve footprint
b: After Senate President Stuart Adams asked June 1 for a 75% smaller footprint, developer Kevin O'Leary announced June 4 he would cut about 20,000 of 40,000 acres. He had earlier called the request outrageous and did not commit to lower power use.
iw: Smaller footprint, but power demand unchanged and pressure growing

t: Iron County planners approve permit for 1.5-gigawatt Antelope data campus
b: The planning commission unanimously approved a conditional use permit for Pronghorn Development's 640-acre campus west of Cedar City, with up to five buildings and an on-site 1.5-gigawatt gas plant, after months of opposition. The permit is separate from any tax incentives.
iw: Key permit cleared for a large campus with its own power

t: Arizona law lets regulators set minimum bills and contract terms for extra-high-load customers
b: HB 2756 authorizes the Corporation Commission to set rules for very large power users such as data centers, including minimum bills and contract terms, and requires utilities to report on new interconnection requests.
iw: Opens the door to stricter cost and contract rules

t: Residents sue to put Stratos agreements on Box Elder ballot
b: The Box Elder Accountability Referendum group appealed the county attorney's rejection in 1st District Court, arguing the resolutions were legislative. The county and developer O'Leary Digital moved to dismiss in late July; no hearing had been scheduled as of early August.
iw: Could force a public vote, though odds are uncertain

w: Alliance for a Better Utah and five Box Elder residents
t: Alliance for a Better Utah sues MIDA over Stratos approvals
b: A civil-rights suit in 3rd District Court argues the MIDA law strips residents' referendum rights and that two senators' seats on MIDA's board violate the constitution. Defendants include MIDA, the county commission, Sen. Stuart Adams and Sen. Jerry Stevenson.
iw: Challenges the legal basis of the fast-track approval

t: Gordon signs 'Data Centers the Wyoming Way' executive order
b: Executive Order 2026-03 sets a framework directing agencies to protect ratepayers, water, wildlife and communities, require public participation, and expect developers to cover their power costs. It also welcomes investment and cites national security.
iw: Welcomes projects but adds cost, water and transparency expectations

t: Boulder County adopts six-month pause on data center applications
b: Commissioners unanimously stopped accepting planning applications for data centers (and detention centers) in unincorporated areas while staff draft land-use code changes. A public hearing was set for July 2.
iw: New applications frozen for up to six months

t: Steinmetz asks lawmakers to poll on special session for data centers
b: The senator requested a poll on a session focused on data centers, large electric loads and water, calling the governor's order a fast track. Senate President Bo Biteman called a session premature. No special session had been reported.
iw: Pressure for state limits before the 2027 session

t: Tooele County starts review of data center rules and energy excise tax
b: Resolution 2026-18 directs staff and planners to recommend data center land-use rules, an energy excise tax and development-overlay standards. The county said it had approved no data center and has no specific regulations yet. Exact meeting date needs confirming.
iw: Rule-writing under way; no pause or approval yet

w: Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power (Black Hills Energy)
t: Black Hills asks Wyoming PSC for large-customer transmission cost mechanism
b: The filing seeks a Large Customer Transmission Cost Adjustment Mechanism and changes to related tariffs, aimed at assigning transmission costs to very large customers such as data centers. The PSC noticed the application July 7; a decision is pending.
iw: Shifts more transmission cost onto large data center customers

t: Cox signs executive order setting a 'higher bar' for large data centers
b: Executive Order 2026-03 directs state agencies to apply a framework protecting Great Salt Lake water, ratepayers and air quality, mitigating wildlife impacts and allowing public comment. Cox said it could delay Stratos.
iw: Stricter state review, mostly applying existing laws

t: Box Elder attorney rules Stratos resolutions cannot go to voters
b: County Attorney Stephen Hadfield found the consent and interlocal-agreement resolutions administrative, not legislative, so not referable. The county said repeal would cost guaranteed revenue of $5.4 million a year. Sponsors vowed to appeal.
iw: Blocks a ballot challenge to the project approvals

t: Wyoming PSC proposes rules for non-public-utility power generators
b: The commission gave notice of intent to adopt Chapter 6, a process to decide when arrangements generating electricity for retail customers are exempt from utility rules. A public hearing was set for Aug. 5; adoption is pending.
iw: Could ease off-grid generation for data centers

t: Iron County pauses new data center and large solar applications for 180 days
b: Ordinance 2026-13 halts new applications for data centers, their power plants and large solar projects while the county rewrites its rules. One already-complete project was not covered. Planners proposed new restrictions in early October.
iw: Applications frozen up to six months, pending rules

t: Cheyenne council rejects one-year data center moratorium, 8-1
b: After about four hours of public comment, split roughly evenly, only sponsor Mark Moody voted for the pause. Some outlets reported 9-1; the Greater Cheyenne Chamber says the official record shows 8-1. Opponents cited jobs and existing studies.
iw: Pause rejected in the state's biggest data center market

w: Utah Legislature Natural Resources Interim Committee
t: Utah interim committee votes to study data center impacts
b: The Natural Resources Interim Committee agreed to add a study of data center impacts, on a motion by Rep. Doug Owens. Republicans on the panel did not oppose it. The scope was not yet defined.
iw: Study only; no rule change yet

t: Jefferson County pauses new data center applications and rezonings until March 2027
b: Commissioners voted May 19 for a 10-month pause on new data center applications and rezonings, through March 2027. Land already zoned for data centers through a Planned Development is excluded only if the facility is at least 1,500 feet from any dwelling. Only one such district exists.
iw: Ten-month freeze in a large metro-area county

t: Pocatello hearing examiner denies permit for $2.6 billion AI data center
b: Examiner Kathleen Lewis found Lex Developments' application for the former Hoku plant failed three of seven criteria: public facilities, environmental impact and public welfare. She said power, water and air studies should come before another application.
iw: Project-killing decision for Idaho's largest proposed campus

t: Sabey ends Butte land deal after REC Silicon uses purchase right
b: Sabey terminated its agreement to buy about 606 acres for two planned 500,000-square-foot data centers on May 13, after REC Silicon exercised a right of first refusal on 627.8 acres including much of the site. Sabey said it is still looking in southwest Montana.
iw: Project lost its site over land rights, though Sabey seeks others

t: Colorado Senate committee shelves large-load data center regulation bill SB26-102
b: The sponsor asked the committee to postpone her bill indefinitely, and it agreed unanimously, after a compromise with incentives fell through. She plans to reintroduce it next session.
iw: Proposed energy and water rules died for this year

t: Colorado committee kills data center tax-incentive bill HB26-1030
b: The House committee voted 11-2 to postpone the industry-backed incentive bill indefinitely. It would have offered long sales-tax exemptions for large investments. Colorado still has no state data center incentive.
iw: Developers lose a hoped-for state tax break

t: BLM fast-tracks federal approval of Project Jupiter gas pipeline across 16 miles
b: Using a 14-day emergency environmental review, the Bureau of Land Management authorized the Green Chile pipeline across about 16 miles of public land and began finalizing rights-of-way with Transwestern. Federal commission review and state-land access were still unresolved.
iw: Federal fast track for the project's gas supply

t: Maricopa County approves military permit for Project Baccara data center near Luke base
b: Supervisors voted 4-1 for the permit required near military bases. The 160-acre plan has two data centers and a 700-megawatt gas plant. Hundreds of residents opposed it, and air-quality approval was still pending.
iw: Key permit cleared for a large bring-your-own-power campus

t: Box Elder commissioners approve Stratos project area and MIDA agreement
b: Commissioners voted unanimously on May 4 for two resolutions: consent to MIDA's project area and an interlocal agreement transferring land-use authority for 50 years. Large crowds protested, and commissioners said the state left them little choice.
iw: Local consent clears the way for a huge campus, but not permits

w: Pima County Superior Court and Marana
t: Courts uphold rejection of Marana data center referendum petitions
b: A judge ruled the town clerk was right to reject two petitions against January's rezoning, and that the sponsor could not withdraw them. The state Court of Appeals later affirmed. No ballot vote is scheduled.
iw: Rezoning stays in place after referendum challenge failed

t: Judge rejects farmers' challenge to Kuna's approval of 620-acre data center
b: Judge James Cawthon denied judicial review of the 3-2 council vote that rezoned land for Diode Ventures' Gemstone Technology Park, finding no disqualifying conflict of interest. The farmers appealed to the Idaho Supreme Court in June.
iw: Rezoning for a large campus survives a legal challenge

t: Duchesne County rejects appeals of Nine Mile data center permits
b: Commissioners denied residents' appeals of the April 2 planning approvals for the Nine Mile data center and related gas, solar and produced-water permits; the first appeal was denied for lack of standing. Appellants said they would seek court remedies.
iw: Permits stay in place after appeals fail

t: MIDA board approves Stratos data center project area in Box Elder County
b: The state authority created a roughly 40,000-acre project area for Kevin O'Leary's data center and power campus. This is a project-area approval, not full construction approval. MIDA can override county zoning. The developer later said it would halve the footprint to about 20,000 acres.
iw: Fast-track land-use approval that bypasses county zoning

t: Juab County planners approve permit for $10 billion Nebo North data center
b: The planning commission approved a conditional use permit for a campus of about 3 million square feet near Mona after a hearing residents say lasted four minutes. Neighbors learned later; in September commissioners were unsure they could cancel the permit.
iw: Major permit cleared with little public notice

t: Judge dismisses open-meeting lawsuit over Project Blue rezoning
b: A Pima County judge ruled the county did not violate open meeting law in rezoning the land, even though the agenda did not name the data center. The opposition coalition said it would appeal.
iw: Rezoning for a built-out campus survives a legal challenge

w: Idaho Legislature and Gov. Brad Little
t: Idaho law requires PUC-approved contracts for new loads of 50 megawatts or more
b: HB 911, signed April 10, sets a no-harm test, cost allocation and financial security for utilities serving new large loads such as data centers. It took effect July 1 after passing the House 65-3 and Senate 34-1.
iw: Cost-recovery and security requirements for large loads

t: Cochise County adopts data center zoning rules instead of a moratorium
b: Supervisors voted 3-0 to require special use authorization, noise studies, water-use plans and proof of power supply, and to mostly bar potable water for cooling. They did not take up the 120-day pause planning commissioners recommended 5-4 in March.
iw: Clear rules and stricter approval, but no pause

t: Weld County adopts data center zoning code and bars them from agricultural land
b: Ordinance 2026-01 passed 4-1. Light industrial zones need a Use by Special Review; medium and heavy industrial need site plan review. The 50-megawatt figure limits backup generation, not total power use. Proof of water and an electric will-serve letter are required.
iw: Clear permitting path with water and power proof required

w: Idaho Legislature and Gov. Brad Little
t: Idaho law restricts consumptive water cooling for new data centers
b: HB 895 bars data centers that begin construction on or after July 1, 2026 from consuming water for cooling unless it comes from a municipal or water district system. It passed the House 58-10 and Senate 32-1.
iw: New projects must use closed-loop cooling or municipal water

t: Idaho bill to narrow data center tax breaks dies without House concurrence
b: HB 897 would have limited the sales tax exemption for new data centers to server equipment and added utility cost-recovery and water-notice rules. It passed the House 68-0 and the Senate 34-0 as amended, but the House never voted on the changes.
iw: Broad state tax breaks stay for at least another year

t: NorthWestern asks PSC to approve large-load tariff for data centers
b: The proposal covers new customers of 5 megawatts or more, with minimum service terms, billing requirements, collateral and termination costs, and PSC review of agreements for the largest. Many parties, including DEQ, sought to intervene. A decision is pending.
iw: Minimum bills, collateral and exit fees raise developer costs

w: Idaho Power and Idaho Public Utilities Commission
t: Idaho Power asks PUC to review cost-of-service rules for new large loads
b: The March 31 petition opens a docket on how costs are allocated among customer classes, including new large loads such as data centers. The PUC set a technical hearing for Jan. 19, 2027 and is taking written comments until Dec. 14.
iw: Could raise cost allocation for large new customers

t: Army picks CyrusOne for exclusive talks on Dugway data center
b: The Army conditionally selected CyrusOne to negotiate a lease for a hyperscale data center on about 1,201 acres at Dugway Proving Ground, targeting fiscal 2029. The developer must supply its own power and water; an Army Corps environmental review is pending.
iw: Federal-land fast track for a large campus

t: Utah law requires large new data centers to report water use
b: HB 76 makes new data centers over 10,000 square feet that expect to use 75 or more acre-feet of water a year report plans before construction and use annually after. Gov. Cox signed it March 23; it took effect May 6, covering projects after July 1.
iw: New disclosure duty with modest cost

t: Utah narrows what the state engineer can weigh in water-right protests
b: HB 60, signed March 23 and effective May 6, limits the state engineer to beneficial use and water quantity, quality and availability when judging public welfare. Critics said it weakens protests like those filed against Stratos's first water application.
iw: Broad public-welfare objections carry less weight

t: Judge lets lawsuit over Project Jupiter's $165 billion bonds proceed
b: Judge Jennifer DeLaney denied the county's motion to dismiss a suit alleging commissioners approved the bonds on an incomplete application, though a March 24 ruling refused to stay the ordinances. Yucca Growth Infrastructure and Green Chile Ventures were allowed to join.
iw: Incentive approval stays under court review

t: Provo council unanimously denies data center overlay for East Bay site
b: The council voted 7-0 against rezoning a parcel for a proposed grid-powered data center, despite a planning commission recommendation to approve. Members cited location and wanted the city's economic plan finished first. The developer may reapply.
iw: Project-killing vote in a Utah County city

t: Utah law limits local incentives for large data centers and allows county energy tax
b: HB 507, signed in March, bars local incentives for large data centers from May 2027 unless they use a state-approved zone or regional authority. Property-tax incentives are generally capped at 60% of new county revenue and never exceed 80%. Counties may levy an energy excise tax up to 6%.
iw: Subsidies restricted and a county energy tax allowed

t: Lea County adopts first data center regulations requiring closed-loop cooling
b: Commissioners unanimously approved the first of several planned revisions for data centers, including closed-loop or similar cooling to avoid drawing drinking-water supplies. The county said developers had approached it over two years; New Era's Caprock campus was announced in November.
iw: Clear water rules set before projects arrive

t: Mayes challenges regulators' approval of TEP deal to power Project Blue
b: She argues the Corporation Commission, which approved the contract 4-1 on Dec. 3, 2025, gave away its rate-setting power by letting TEP and the developer adjust rate schedules. A judge heard the case in September and had not ruled.
iw: Legal challenge to a key power contract

t: Senate passes microgrid oversight bill 22-20; House lets it die
b: SB 235 would have held large private microgrids, such as Project Jupiter's, to the Energy Transition Act's renewable standards and barred shifting their costs to utility customers. It passed the Senate Feb. 14 but the House postponed it indefinitely.
iw: Rules for data center microgrids did not advance

t: Bernalillo County sets conditions for data centers seeking incentives
b: Commissioners voted 4-1 for a resolution requiring data centers that want county incentives to offset water use, use renewable power, hire locally at set wage floors and pay minimum taxes. Projects that skip incentives can sidestep it.
iw: Raises the bar for county subsidies, not a ban

t: Environmental law center sues Doña Ana County over closed session before Project Jupiter vote
b: A new Open Meetings Act suit says commissioners paused the Sept. 19 hearing for a closed session without stating its subject, then approved $165 billion in bonds. It is separate from an earlier suit challenging the bonds themselves.
iw: Could void the county's approval of the project's tax incentives

t: Butte commissioners extend Sabey data center land deal six months, 9-3
b: The council moved the closing deadline for 606 acres from Feb. 11 to Aug. 11, short of the one year Sabey sought, and required two-thirds council approval for any final land transfer. Sabey terminated the deal May 13.
iw: Extension was overtaken when Sabey ended the land deal

t: Navajo LeChee Chapter unanimously opposes Page's land sale for data center
b: The resolution says Page did not consult nearby Navajo residents or weigh risks to water and the environment. Corner Post reports the Coppermine and Kaibito chapters passed similar resolutions.
iw: Adds tribal opposition to a proposed 1-gigawatt campus

t: HB 2467 to repeal data center tax break and set water limits withdrawn
b: The bill would have repealed the incentive, required renewable power with battery storage after 2026, and capped cooling water use. It was withdrawn from committee on Jan. 22 and died.
iw: Stricter state requirements did not advance

t: Laramie County unanimously approves Crusoe data center and Tallgrass power plant site plans
b: Site plans cover Project Jade, a 1.8-gigawatt first phase that could scale far higher, and a gas plant of up to 2.7 gigawatts south of Cheyenne. The campus was later renamed Project Tembo. Future phases need new county review.
iw: One of the largest proposed campuses clears county approval

t: Butte commissioners ask PSC for separate rate class for large data center loads
b: The council voted 10-0 to send a letter urging the Public Service Commission to create a separate rate class and binding tariffs for large electric loads, protecting existing customers. The county has no authority over electric rates.
iw: Local officials push regulators toward stricter large-load rules

t: Chandler council unanimously rejects proposed AI data center
b: The council voted against clearing the way for an AI data center after residents raised noise, water and quality-of-life concerns. The meeting drew a large crowd opposed to the project.
iw: Project-killing vote in a major Phoenix suburb

t: Page council votes 5-2 to sell 500 acres for possible data center
b: The sale to Huntley LLC sets a feasibility period and does not approve a data center. Residents' referendum petition was disqualified on technical grounds, and opponents continue to organize.
iw: Land secured for a possible 1-gigawatt campus

t: Doña Ana County approves $165 billion bonds and tax breaks for Project Jupiter
b: Commissioners voted 4-1 after a closed session and seven hours of public comment to approve $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds for the Santa Teresa campus planned for Oracle and OpenAI. The vote later drew Open Meetings Act lawsuits.
iw: Decades-long tax relief clears a giant campus

t: Chaves County approves Zenith Volts data center campus south of Roswell
b: Commissioners approved the project, which the county describes as a special use permit for a 1,265-megawatt solar facility to power a 300-acre data center. Company figures put the data center at 1.25 to 1.3 gigawatts on an 8,400- to 8,500-acre site south of Roswell. The county offered no incentives.
iw: Large off-grid campus approved without opposition or incentives

t: State reviews QTS request for 98 more diesel generators at Aurora data center
b: QTS applied in July 2025 to add 98 backup generators to 40 already installed. State air regulators were reviewing the application as of July 2026, with a public comment period expected. NRDC cited ozone concerns.
iw: Air permit could limit backup power at a hyperscale site

t: APS rate case seeks over 45% increase for data centers and other extra-large users
b: APS says the proposal makes large customers pay their costs of service. The hearing began May 18, 2026. A Corporation Commission decision is expected by the end of 2026, and rates could land below the request.
iw: Higher power costs for large users if approved

t: Montana extends data center property tax incentive to 2037
b: HB 424 extends the window to begin qualified data center construction to 2037 and adds on-site generation and storage property to the reduced-rate treatment. Data center property is taxed at 0.9%.
iw: Longer tax incentive and self-generation treatment

t: Montana Right to Compute Act limits government restrictions on data centers
b: SB 212 passed 50-0 in the Senate and 61-38 in the House. It requires restrictions on computing resources to be narrowly tailored to a compelling interest. It does not ban local zoning outright; how much authority counties keep is unsettled, and local officials say it constrains moratoria.
iw: Legal shield against local bans and strict zoning
